aboutme.body: Turkish has no separate "am". You add an ending to the word instead.
aboutme.title: No word for "am"

argue.body: The bare verb is a command to one person. Add -me or -ma to say "don't".
argue.title: Giving orders

around.body: The ending -de or -da means in or at. The question word nerede is simply "at where".
around.title: Where: nerede

athome.body: Put the describing word before the noun, as in English. Put it after, and it becomes a sentence: there is no word for "is".
athome.title: Describing things

bazaar.body: Add mı, mi, mu or mü after the word you're asking about. It is written separately and its vowel follows vowel harmony.
bazaar.title: Asking yes/no questions

bignum.body: Say the big part first, then the small part, with nothing in between.
bignum.title: Building numbers

cafe.body: There is no separate word for a or an. Bir does both jobs, and lütfen usually comes last.
cafe.title: Bir means one, and a

can.body: Slip -ebil or -abil into a verb for "can". For "can't", the short form uses -eme or -ama.
can.title: Can and can't

celebrate.body: Olsun means "may it be". It turns a noun or adjective into a wish, which is why so many set phrases end with it.

examples.en: may it be past (get well soon)

celebrate.title: May it be: olsun

colors.body: Olan means "the one that is". Add the object ending -ı when it is the thing you want.
colors.title: The blue one

days.body: Add günü, "its day", to say on a day. Without it you are just naming the day.
days.title: On Monday

drama.body: Drama characters live on short reactions. Tone does the work: the same tamam can be calm, annoyed or heartbroken.
drama.title: Tiny words, big feelings

famdrama.body: Turks call older people by family titles even when they are not related. It is warm and respectful.
famdrama.title: Everyone is family

family.body: The same -m ending from before: add it to a family word to make it yours.
family.title: My family

feelings.body: The same "I am" ending works on feelings. Its vowel follows vowel harmony.
feelings.title: I am + feeling

flirt.body: Add -sın, -sin, -sun or -sün to an adjective to say "you are".
flirt.title: You are: -sın

goodbyes.body: Who says what depends on who is leaving. The one who leaves says hoşça kal, "stay well". The one who stays answers güle güle, "go smiling".
goodbyes.title: Two goodbyes

greet.body: Turkish spelling is regular: every letter has one sound and no letter is silent, except ğ. If you can read it, you can say it.
greet.title: Read it as it's written

have.body: There is no verb "to have". Say "my thing exists": the my-ending, then var or yok.
have.title: I have: my + var

heartbreak.body: Add -ma or -me to a command and it becomes "don't".
heartbreak.title: Don't: -ma and -me

help.body: End a request with misiniz or musunuz to make it a polite "could you".
help.title: Asking politely

here.body: One ending covers in, on and at. It follows vowel harmony: -da after a, ı, o, u and -de after e, i, ö, ü.
here.title: In, on, at: -da and -de

honour.body: -meyeceğim or -mayacağım on a verb means "I will not". It is long, but you will hear it in every oath.
honour.title: I will not

hotel.body: Var means there is, or I have. Yok is the opposite. Two tiny words you will use every day.
hotel.title: Var and yok

hungry.body: -yorum means "I am doing". Slip -m- in before it and it becomes "I am not doing".
hungry.title: Saying no inside the verb

jobs.body: Add the I-am ending straight onto the job. No word for "a" and no word for "am".
jobs.title: I am a…

likes.body: When you like or want one particular thing, it takes -ı, -i, -u or -ü. After a vowel a y slips in.
likes.title: Liking a specific thing

love.body: Pet names use the "my" ending: can (soul) becomes canım, aşk (love) becomes aşkım. Friends and family use canım too, not only couples.
love.title: My dear, my love

magic.body: Teşekkür ederim is polite and safe everywhere. With friends you'll hear teşekkürler or sağ ol.
magic.title: Formal or casual

makeup.body: Özür dilerim is a real apology. Pardon is for bumping into someone or squeezing past.
makeup.title: Two kinds of sorry

meet.body: Turkish adds endings instead of separate words. Add -m (with a helping vowel) to say "my". The vowel copies the last vowel of the word: this is vowel harmony.
meet.title: "My" is an ending

myday.body: The -yorum ending you met for "I'm eating" covers habits too. Turkish uses it for what you do every day.
myday.title: Everyday actions

num1.body: After a number the noun stays singular. The number already says how many.
num1.title: No plural after numbers

order.body: Put the thing you want first and the verb last. Turkish verbs like to come at the end.
order.title: I want: istiyorum

palace.body: At court nobody is addressed by name. You add the "my" ending to the title, which is why you hear sultanım and hünkârım all the time.
palace.title: Titles carry "my"

plans.body: Add -alım or -elim to a verb to say "let's". Add mı or mi to turn it into "shall we?".
plans.title: Let's: -alım and -elim

qwords.body: A question word sits where the answer would go, and you do not add mı. The word itself makes it a question.
qwords.title: Question words

snd1.body: The little tail changes the sound. C on its own sounds like the j in jam.
snd1.title: Ç is "ch", Ş is "sh"

snd2.body: İ with a dot is the ee in see. I without a dot is a short "uh", like the e in open. They are different letters, and the capitals keep the dot too: İ and I.
snd2.title: Two different i's

snd3.body: Say "e" with rounded lips and you get Ö. Say "ee" with rounded lips and you get Ü.

examples.en: like the u in French tu

snd3.title: Round your lips

snd4.body: Ğ never makes a sound of its own. It just stretches the vowel before it.
snd4.title: Ğ is silent

teatime.body: Elinize sağlık is the polite form. To a friend or family member you say ellerine sağlık. Both thank someone for what their hands made.
teatime.title: Health to your hands

time.body: Say saat, then the number. Asking is just saat kaç: "hour how many".
time.title: Telling the time

tomorrow.body: Add -eceğim or -acağım for "I will". The ğ is silent, so it sounds like a long vowel.
tomorrow.title: The future: -eceğim

tough.body: -eceksin or -acaksın on a verb means "you will". Short, final, and a favorite of every tough guy.
tough.title: You will

unwell.body: Name the body part with the my-ending, then ağrıyor, "is hurting".
unwell.title: My head hurts

warriors.body: One word with many jobs: thanks, okay, goodbye, so be it. It is often said with a hand on the heart.
warriors.title: Eyvallah

wishes.body: Turkish has a ready phrase for eating, working, being ill, even getting a haircut. Using them is simply good manners.
wishes.title: A wish for every moment

yesterday.body: Add -dim, -dım, -dum or -düm for "I did". After p, ç, t, k, s, ş, h, f the d hardens to t.
yesterday.title: The past: -dim
